name: Keycloak
description: An identity and access management server: single sign-on over OpenID Connect and SAML, multi-factor sign-in, user federation with LDAP and Active Directory, and brokering to other identity providers. It is configured through an admin console and organised into realms.
backing: A Cloud Native Computing Foundation project, started at Red Hat, which still does much of the development and sells a supported build

maturity.rationale: More than a decade of releases, a CNCF project since 2023, and the login layer of a great many companies, universities and public bodies. Upgrades between major versions still need the migration notes read first.

selfHosting.summary: Runs as a container or on the JVM in front of PostgreSQL. A test instance takes minutes; a production one takes real care: TLS and hostname settings, a database with backups, a second node if a login outage would stop the company, and the habit of reading upgrade notes. After that, every app has to be connected to it.

requirements.notes: Plus a PostgreSQL database. Allow more memory for thousands of active sessions.

managedHosting.label: Cloud-IAM
managedHosting.note: Managed Keycloak from a French provider

managedHosting.label: Phase Two
managedHosting.note: Managed Keycloak with extra organisation features

strengths: Works with nearly every app: OpenID Connect, SAML and years of written-up integrations
Signs people in against an existing LDAP or Active Directory, so nobody has to be re-created
No paid edition: clustering, fine-grained authorisation and everything else are in the open build
weaknesses: A lot to learn before the first app signs in: realms, clients, flows and mappers
No built-in way to push accounts to other apps (SCIM) or to protect apps that lack single sign-on; both need add-ons
The admin console and default login pages are functional rather than friendly

featureNotes.legacy-apps: Pair it with a gateway such as oauth2-proxy
featureNotes.multi-tenant: Realms, and organisations within a realm
